ch.str: Quantitative traders strip out all the narrative. To them, a stock is just a time series — patterns, autocorrelations, mean reversion, momentum signals. The market becomes a mathematical system with exploitable inefficiencies. Find the signal in the noise before others do, and you win.

ch.n: The Efficient Market Hypothesis argues t
ch.str: The Efficient Market Hypothesis argues that all known information is already priced in. No analysis can consistently beat the market, because prices move randomly in response to new, unpredictable information. If this is true, then the best strategy is simply: own everything, pay nothing in fees, and wait. Most active funds lose to the index over 10 years.

ch.n: Markets are a competition between partic
ch.str: Markets are a competition between participants with asymmetric information. Insiders know the earnings before you do. Big institutions pay for satellite imagery, credit card transaction flows, and sentiment data feeds. Fast traders see your order before it fully executes. The edge is always about information — its quality, speed, and interpretation.

Whatever your philosophy — behavioral, quantitative, or somewhere in between — trading is ultimately about separating real, exploitable patterns from random fluctuations. The next sessions give you the foundation to start.

ch.n: At its core, a stock market is a marketp
ch.str: At its core, a stock market is a marketplace where buyers and sellers trade ownership pieces of companies.

ch.n: A company needs money to grow. Instead o
ch.str: A company needs money to grow. Instead of borrowing from a bank, it can sell small pieces of itself — called shares — to the public.

ch.n: When you buy a share, you own a tiny fra
ch.str: When you buy a share, you own a tiny fraction of that company. If the company does well, your share is worth more. If it does badly, it's worth less.

ch.n: The Egyptian Exchange is the regulated m
ch.str: The Egyptian Exchange is the regulated marketplace where all this buying and selling happens in real time, under FRA supervision.

ch.n: You can't walk into EGX and trade direct
ch.str: You can't walk into EGX and trade directly. You need a licensed intermediary — EFG Hermes — to place orders on your behalf.

ch.str: How Is a Stock Price Formed?

ch.str: Price is simply what the last buyer agreed to pay the last seller. Supply vs. demand in real time.

ch.n: When more people want to buy than sell,
ch.str: When more people want to buy than sell, price rises. When more want to sell, price falls.

ch.n: How Do You Buy or Sell?
ch.str: How Do You Buy or Sell?

ch.n: When you trade, you place an "order" — a
ch.str: When you trade, you place an "order" — an instruction to buy or sell. Different order types give you different control.

ch.n: Buy NOW at whatever the market offers. G
ch.str: Buy NOW at whatever the market offers. Guarantees execution, not price. Used when speed matters.

ch.n: Only buy at EGP 65 or lower. Guarantees
ch.str: Only buy at EGP 65 or lower. Guarantees price, not execution. The trade only happens if market reaches your target.

ch.n: If price falls to EGP 55, automatically
ch.str: If price falls to EGP 55, automatically sell to cut losses. Critical for risk management — lets you sleep at night.

ch.n: Triggered at the stop price, but only ex
ch.str: Triggered at the stop price, but only executes within your limit range. More control, but can miss in fast markets.

ch.n: ↳ The order book below is the real-world
ch.str: ↳ The order book below is the real-world version of the supply vs. demand curves above — captured at a single moment in time, at actual price levels, with real quantities waiting to trade.

ch.n: The order book shows pending buy (bid) a
ch.str: The order book shows pending buy (bid) and sell (ask) orders stacked by price. The spread is where market makers earn.

ch.n: A price chart is a visual record of a st
ch.str: A price chart is a visual record of a stock's price over time. It's the primary tool traders use to understand market behaviour. There are several types — each shows different levels of information.

ch.n: The simplest price chart. It connects on
ch.str: The simplest price chart. It connects only the closing prices of each period — one dot per day (or hour, or minute), joined by a line.

ch.n: Good for seeing the big picture trend. B
ch.str: Good for seeing the big picture trend. But it throws away a lot of information — you don't see what happened during each period.

ch.n: − Shows only close — ignores open, high,
ch.str: − Shows only close — ignores open, high, low

ch.n: NOTE: Volume is independent of chart typ
ch.str: NOTE: Volume is independent of chart type — it's always displayed as a separate bar subplot below any price chart.

ch.n: Price and volume are two separate dimens
ch.str: Price and volume are two separate dimensions of information. Neither tells the full story alone.

ch.n: Volume measures how many shares changed
ch.str:
Volume measures how many shares changed hands in a given period. It answers: how much conviction was behind this price move?

● Green volume bar = price closed higher than previous day — buyers were in control.

● Red volume bar = price closed lower than previous day — sellers were in control.

A large price move on high volume is a strong signal. The same move on low volume is weak and likely to reverse.

ch.n: The market has many different types of p
ch.str: The market has many different types of participants — each with different goals, time horizons, and strategies.

ch.n: EGX launched its formal Market Maker pro
ch.str: EGX launched its formal Market Maker program in January 2019. Today, only one firm is registered — Beltone Market Maker (code 5095). In mature markets like the US, dozens of market makers compete on every liquid stock, which is part of why their spreads stay tight and liquidity is deep. On EGX, most liquidity comes from natural buyers and sellers meeting in the order book — one reason spreads can widen and liquidity can dry up faster on news.
EGX — TRADING BY INVESTOR TYPE (SOURCE: EGX / ZAWYA, 2025)
Egyptian retail investors dominate at ~82% of all transactions — institutional and foreign participation remains low.
Essential vocabulary you'll encounter constantly. Know these before Session 2.

ch.n: A market trending upward — prices rising
ch.str: A market trending upward — prices rising 20%+ from recent lows. Optimism dominates.

ch.n: A market trending downward — prices fall
ch.str: A market trending downward — prices falling 20%+ from recent highs. Pessimism dominates.

ch.n: How easily you can buy or sell without m
ch.str: How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price. High liquidity = easy to trade.

ch.n: How much price fluctuates. High volatili
ch.str: How much price fluctuates. High volatility = bigger swings = more risk and opportunity.

ch.n: Bid = highest buyers offer. Ask = lowest
ch.str: Bid = highest buyers offer. Ask = lowest sellers accept. The spread is the market maker's profit.

ch.n: Total value of a company = share price ×
ch.str: Total value of a company = share price × number of shares outstanding.

ch.n: A portion of company profits paid to sha
ch.str: A portion of company profits paid to shareholders. Not all companies pay dividends.

ch.n: Borrowing shares to sell now, hoping to
ch.str: Borrowing shares to sell now, hoping to buy cheaper later. Betting on a price decline.

ch.n: Initial Public Offering — when a private
ch.str: Initial Public Offering — when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time.
